strengths: Addresses a meaningful problem: jointly choosing which variables to intervene on and which observations to use as context. Integrating causal policy-scope selection with continuous-domain Bayesian optimization is practically relevant.

The motivating example in Figure 1 is analytically convincing: controlling X1 as −C achieves expected reward 1/3, whereas jointly controlling X1 and X2 achieves zero. This clearly demonstrates why intervention-scope selection matters.

Experiments consider cases where the baselines can and cannot attain the optimum, use 110 seeds, and report uncertainty intervals. The paper also acknowledges the configuration where contextual BO converges faster.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited. The algorithm combines previously established POMPS selection criteria, HEBO, and standard UCB, without a new structural characterization or substantial modification of these components. The practical extension is useful, but its significance beyond existing mixed-policy-scope research needs stronger evidence.

The UCB justification in Section 4.2 is incomplete: each arm's reward distribution changes as its HEBO optimizer learns. Observing that rewards become stationary at optimality does not establish that the coupled procedure reaches optimality. Decreasing average regret over 700 iterations also cannot establish asymptotic sublinear regret or support the conclusion that the method always reaches the optimum.

Support for general mixed policy scopes is insufficiently specified. Definition 3.1 permits action-specific contexts and sequential observation/intervention dependencies, whereas Section 4 optimizes a joint action vector given a fixed combined context. The paper does not explain how information constraints are preserved. Moreover, Appendix C's CoBO baseline conditions interventions on Xt variables on C5, despite Xt → C5; this creates a cycle under Definition 3.1 unless a different observation protocol is intended.

The comparisons do not isolate the contribution of UCB scope selection. In the PSA experiments, CoCa-BO has only one candidate scope, so its improved behavior cannot demonstrate the effectiveness of its scope selector. Comparisons using identical POMPS sets and HEBO models, with uniform allocation or alternative scope selectors, are missing. Baseline optimizer configurations are also insufficiently documented to separate improvements from the search space and optimization backend.

Evaluation is restricted to two small synthetic graph families and an enlarged synthetic example with deliberately redundant variables. CoCa-BO encounters only one or two candidate scopes. Consequently, the experiments provide little evidence about performance with many competing scopes, the computational cost of enumerating POMPSes, or applicability to realistic optimization tasks.

The benchmark specifications contain consequential inconsistencies. Appendix A.2's displayed PSA equation contains no Cancer term, yet the subsequent substitution introduces it; the claimed sum-of-squares objective and zero optimum therefore do not follow from the written SCM. Appendix C also defines C4 through itself, contradicting the displayed acyclic graph. These may be transcription errors, but they prevent verification of the benchmark objectives and regret references.

Reproducibility is incomplete: UCB exploration settings, initialization procedures, several intervention domains, and baseline configurations are not adequately specified. Although code sharing is mentioned, no repository link is provided in the manuscript.
